p: The system requirements review passed with four actions, and HEARTH's baseline was set at three hundred and ninety six requirements.
Helen said it was the first set she'd read that sounded like it had met a crew.
Wes had three changes waiting for Friday's board: a hatch handle on both sides, seat track down both sides of the aisle, and every harness run overhead.
Then Nadia found his revision C hatch drawing on the plotter, dated before anyone decided the changes, with all three drawn in and the aisle eleven centimeters narrower than the tape.
Her father had texted that she'd missed Sunday with Callie, so Sunday at noon is in her calendar now with an alarm on it.
Wes Harland. Chief engineer. He drew his changes before the board decided them.
Jun Takeda. Keeps the model. He presented the trace at the review.
Tiago Ferreira. Test lead, now planning how to check every line.
Amara Osei. Program manager. She shook Nadia's hand after the review.
Odette. Safety engineer. She asked what has to break for the hatch to open.
Helen Cho-Ramirez. Halo's crew lead. She asked for sixty seconds, knowing better.
New in this chapter: Ansel Teague.
Chapter four. Shape of the System.

Revision C had come off Wes's plotter three days before the requirements review. On Friday of week six Nadia took it to his desk at a quarter past eight, before the board met, before she could talk herself out of it. She'd practiced the first sentence in the hallway. You drew this before anyone decided it.

Wes's desk was the one by the windows. He had a breakfast burrito going and the structures schedule up on both screens. His paperweight was a test coupon from a pressure vessel, bent in half on purpose.
She spread the sheet over his keyboard. This is really clean work, she said.
So that was what came out instead.
It's a hatch, Wes said. I've drawn forty.
The aisle's eleven centimeters narrower than the tape.
Seat track down both sides. Crew needs somewhere to clip stuff that isn't the floor. He found note eight with a finger that had salsa on it. Every cargo module had it.
Cargo didn't sleep in there. She didn't say that either. She said, Can we talk about the aisle?

We're talking. There was a photo pinned over his desk of the 2019 cargo module in the test cell, the one that leaked at the hatch seal. Wes had found that leak himself. Everybody at FRO knew the story, mostly from Wes. He'd been right about almost everything since she got here, which made this harder.
Her stomach did its usual thing. The next word was supposed to be no. She was already shopping for a nicer one.
Colleen's Flight Notes: what it does, then where it goes.

Colleen volunteered Saturdays at the air museum at old Lowry, and she met Nadia beside a jet trainer with an access panel off its side. Behind the panel ran a bundle of wire as thick as a wrist, every wire tagged at both ends.
Everybody photographs the cockpit, she said. This is the airplane.
System architecture definition works from the system requirements, and in practice it runs alongside requirements definition, each one shaping the other.

Here's the card for system architecture definition. Its purpose is to work out a few candidate architectures, pick the one or ones that answer what the stakeholders care about and satisfy the system requirements, and describe the choice in views that agree with each other. It takes in the system requirements, the life cycle concepts and scenarios, the constraints, and what's known about the systems around it. It puts out an architecture description: the elements, the interfaces between them, the requirements allocated to each element, the views and models, and the reasons for the choices. Design definition picks it up next and adds the detail to build or buy each element. System analysis checks the candidates, and integration and verification plan around the interfaces.

An architecture has two halves. The functional architecture says what the system must do, broken into functions and the flows between them, with no hardware named. Many sources call this the logical architecture. The physical architecture says which elements will do it and how they connect. Allocation joins the two: each function, and each requirement, goes to the element or elements responsible, often with derived requirements written for each.

Good architecture work looks at more than one candidate. A team that develops one idea and stops has skipped the comparison that gives the choice its meaning. Candidates are judged against the requirements and the stakeholders' concerns, with system analysis supplying the numbers and decision management making the call. A few principles help. Give each element one clear job, and keep its connections to the others few and simple. Architects call that high cohesion and low coupling, and it makes elements easier to test, swap and upgrade. Modularity has a price, often in mass and connectors, so it gets traded like anything else. Starting from a reference architecture, one already proven across an industry, saves time and gives everyone the same words. An architecture framework goes a step further: a standard set of viewpoints, so every architecture in an organization gets described the same way. And anything the system has to live with that can't change, like the station's own power bus, goes in as a constraint, with the interfaces designed around it. When design later finds that an element can't meet what was allocated to it, the finding comes back here, and the allocation or the architecture changes.
Wes drew a good airplane, Colleen said. Now ask him what it's for, one function at a time.

How the exam asks it. Architecture defines elements and interfaces at the system level. Design definition adds the detail to build them. If an answer jumps to detailed design before functions are allocated, it's out of order.

An interface is anywhere two elements exchange something: power, data, heat, fluid, force, or a crew member's hand. Most integration trouble starts at one. An N-squared diagram finds them on purpose. Put the elements on the diagonal. By the usual convention, a mark in an element's row shows what it sends to the element in that column, and a mark in its column shows what it receives. With n elements there are n times one less than n possible one way interfaces, so no pair gets skipped for lack of imagination. Busy rows and columns show the tightly coupled elements. Empty cells are claims too.

Interface management, as a method, means identifying every interface, defining it, controlling it, and verifying that both sides meet it. A definition says what crosses, in what form, at what values, and who owns each side. It lives in interface requirements and an interface control document, or ICD, that both owners agree to. Once it's agreed, the ICD goes under configuration control, so a change takes a change request, an impact assessment, and sign off from both sides.

Interfaces come in kinds. Physical interfaces are the hardware that touches: bolts, connectors, fluid fittings, the berthing ring. Functional interfaces are what passes across: power, heat, data, air. Logical interfaces are what the passing stuff means, such as a message format and what each field says. Human interfaces are where a person reads, reaches, pushes or listens. Internal interfaces sit between elements of your own system. External interfaces cross the boundary to something you don't own, like the station's power bus or the arm's grapple fixture, and you rarely get to set those alone. Interface requirements go into the specifications on both sides, so neither one builds to its own reading. When two organizations own the two sides, an interface control working group brings them together to agree each definition and manage its changes, and the integrator watches the interfaces that run between suppliers, because no single supplier sees both sides. Interface management runs for the whole life of the system, not just until the drawings are signed.

Some programs keep interface data in two documents. An interface requirements document says what each side must provide. The ICD records the agreed design that meets those requirements, down to pin numbers and bolt patterns. Either way, both owners sign, and both documents sit under configuration control.
Two different crews built the front and back of this airplane, Colleen said. The wire works because they agreed on the plug before either one built anything.

How the exam asks it. N-squared: row is output, column is input, and n times one less than n possible cells. A change to an agreed ICD is a configuration management item for both parties, not a quick fix by one.
Colleen climbed into the front seat and pointed at the gauges. Each one showed one thing to the person who needed it.

The architecture description standard, ISO 42010, describes architecture the same way. Stakeholders have concerns. A viewpoint sets the conventions for building a kind of view that frames certain concerns: which models, which notation, which rules. A view applies a viewpoint to this system. The architecture description names the stakeholders and their concerns, and holds the viewpoints, the views, and the reasoning behind them. Helen's crew movement view, the safety office's hazard view, and Tiago's test access view should all come from one model so they can't disagree.

In model based systems engineering the model is the main work product and documents come out of it. In SysML, a block definition diagram shows what the system is made of, an internal block diagram shows how the parts connect through ports, and activity, sequence and state diagrams show behavior. Digital engineering is the wider approach behind all of it: the program's models and data kept in digital form, one authoritative source for each piece of truth, and tools connected so every stage works from the same data instead of copies of it. A digital thread links the data across the life cycle, from requirements to model to CAD, analysis and test, so a change can be followed. A digital twin is a model of one specific built unit kept in step with data from it. HEARTH won't have a twin until there's hardware. Someone also has to decide which copy of the model is the authoritative one, who can read it, and who can change it. That's information management, and on a model based program the model is what it manages.

SysML has nine kinds of diagram, and the exam expects you to know what each is for. Four show structure. The block definition diagram shows what the system is made of. The internal block diagram shows how the parts connect. The package diagram shows how the model itself is organized. The parametric diagram shows the equations that tie values together, like part masses adding up to the module's mass. Four show behavior. The activity diagram shows flows of actions, the sequence diagram shows messages between parts over time, the state machine diagram shows the modes a thing moves between, and the use case diagram shows who uses the system to do what. The ninth, the requirement diagram, shows requirements and how they're derived, satisfied and verified. A diagram is a view into the model, not the model. Change an element once, and every diagram that shows it changes with it.

Models come in many kinds. A physical model is a real object, like a scale model in a wind tunnel, or plywood walls standing on a tape outline. A mathematical model is equations. A simulation runs a model through time. A discrete event simulation handles things that happen at random moments, like crew members reaching a hatch. A Monte Carlo analysis runs a model many times, drawing the uncertain inputs at random from their ranges, and shows the spread of results. Every model is a simplified stand in, built for a purpose. Verifying a model checks that it was built right to its own design. Validating a model checks that it matches reality well enough for its use. A model that's valid for one question may not be valid for the next one, so its assumptions and limits get written down where its users will see them.

How the exam asks it. Viewpoint is the template; view is the product. Concerns belong to stakeholders. Internal block diagram for ports and connections; block definition diagram for hierarchy; parametric for equations; sequence for messages over time; state machine for modes. Verifying a model checks it was built right. Validating it checks it fits reality for its use.
One airplane in a big sky.
This jet was never the system, Colleen said, and patted the panel closed. The system was the jet, the tankers, the radar, the tower, and a thousand people who didn't work for my wing.

A system of systems is made of systems that are independent in operation and in management. Each has its own owner, purpose and life cycle, and could run on its own. In a directed one, the whole is built and managed centrally for a set purpose, and the constituents, though they could still run on their own, normally serve that purpose. In an acknowledged one, there are shared goals and a designated manager, but each constituent keeps its own owner and funding. In a collaborative one, the constituents agree to work together with no central authority. A virtual one has neither a central manager nor an agreed central purpose. Halo Station is close to acknowledged: Halo owns the station's rules, and other companies own the modules.

The marks most often cited come from the systems architect Mark Maier, and there are five. The constituents are independent in operation. They're independent in management. The whole develops over time instead of being finished once. Its important behavior emerges across the constituents. And its parts are usually spread out geographically. The first two are what make it a system of systems at all. The other three describe how one behaves.

What makes a system of systems hard isn't its size. It's that nobody is fully in charge. Each constituent keeps its own owner, budget, schedule and life cycle, and it was usually built for its own purpose first, so its owner makes choices that are right for it and awkward for the whole. Membership changes: modules arrive, vehicles come and go, and the whole keeps changing while it runs. The behavior that matters most, like a crew moving between modules in an emergency, exists only across constituents, so no single owner can test it alone. Requirements for the whole compete with each constituent's own. Life cycles don't line up, so one piece is being designed while another is already flying and a third is getting an upgrade. And in most types, authority runs on agreement more than command, which makes interfaces, shared rules and the working group the main tools. For a constituent like HEARTH, the job is to know where its authority ends, to say early when a station rule collides with its own needs, and to keep its interfaces honest, because the whole depends on them.

Engineering a constituent inside one changes the work. You study the other constituents as they really are, not as their brochures describe them. You treat the behavior of the whole as something to watch in operation, because new behavior can show up any time one member changes on its own. You offer your own changes to the others and time them to their schedules, since in most types nobody can order them to accept. And you keep a working relationship with whoever runs the whole, because shared rules and trust do the job that command does in an ordinary program.

Testing the whole is its own problem. An end to end test across constituents needs every owner to agree to it, and their schedules rarely line up, so programs lean on simulations of the other members, interface test sets that stand in for them, and joint tests at the few moments when everyone can be in the same place. Whatever can't be tested together gets watched closely once it's running.

System analysis supplies the data behind technical decisions. You start from the question, pick a level of detail that fits the decision, write down every assumption, and hand the results, with their uncertainty, to whoever has to decide.

Here's the card for system analysis. Its purpose is to give a rigorous base of data and information for technical understanding and decisions, across the life cycle. It takes in the question from whichever process asked it, along with the models, data and assumptions on hand. It puts out results with their assumptions, limits and uncertainty, recorded so others can check them. They go back to the asker: architecture and design to choose between candidates, decision management to score a trade, risk management to size a risk, and verification when analysis is the method.

Analyses come in a few families. Effectiveness analysis asks how well a candidate meets the MOEs. Cost analysis asks what it costs over its life. Risk analysis asks what could go wrong and how likely it is. Trade analysis puts those side by side. Whatever the family, the level of detail should fit the decision. A rough model that answers the question this week beats a perfect one that answers it after the decision is made.
Before she left, Colleen asked about Jun.

INCOSE's systems engineering competency framework sorts what an engineer needs into core, professional, management, technical and integrating groups, at five levels from awareness through supervised practitioner, practitioner and lead practitioner to expert.
Somebody put your name forward once, she said. Your turn.

How the exam asks it. Clues for a system of systems: constituents with their own owners and missions, behavior that only exists across them, and no single owner of everything. Directed, acknowledged, collaborative, virtual runs from most central control to least. The difficulty comes from independence: no one authority over requirements, money, test or schedule, members that come and go, life cycles that don't line up, and behavior that only shows up across owners.
Wes's three change requests were first on the board's agenda at ten. The drawing had already answered all three.
Structures releases the frame drawings in two weeks, Wes said, or the long lead aluminum slips a month. Amara will tell you the same.
Revision C showed where everything went. The sentence she'd practiced was still out in the hallway. What does Nadia say?
A. Let all nine frames go now, and raise the aisle again at the design review.
B. Hold revision C as a candidate until the functions are mapped, and free safe frames.
C. Approve revision C with the aisle width as an owned, dated item for the trade study.
D. Approve revision C as the architecture, and let structure release all nine frames.

She says it in one breath, which isn't how she rehearsed it. Revision C is a candidate, not the architecture, until they know what the module has to do, and the frames that don't touch the aisle can go now. Wes looks at her for a while. Which frames. She has them circled already. He releases six of nine that afternoon and writes HOLD on the other three in block letters. Two weeks, he says. Then I want my aisle back.

That's the one. Functional and physical architecture develop together, but the functions come first so the elements answer real needs. Treating a drawing as one candidate keeps it honest, and freeing the parts no open function depends on protects the schedule.

Sunday at noon the alarm she'd set went off, and she made the call she'd promised. Monday she and Jun took the big conference room, the one with the old lighting diagram still ghosted under the whiteboard.

Jun had started a function list over the weekend. It was long, and it read like a parts catalog: air rack functions, thermal functions, power functions. That's how Wes splits up the work, he said. So that's how I split up the functions.
What should a functional architecture be built around?
A. Rebuild the list from what HEARTH must do, with no hardware named.
B. Keep Jun's subsystem lists and add a column for crossing functions.
C. Skip the function list and go straight to the physical boxes.
D. Start from FRO's last cargo module function tree and add a crew branch.

Nadia has him start over from what HEARTH must do, with no hardware in it. They put five verbs at the top: keep the crew alive, protect them from hazards, house them, connect to the station, support the module for fifteen years. By Wednesday "protect from hazards" has a branch that runs detect fire, warn the crew, stop the air moving, put it out. None of the boxes has a part number. Jun keeps reaching for one and stopping.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. A functional architecture describes what the system does and the flows between functions, without naming hardware. Organizing it by subsystem bakes in the physical answer and hides functions no subsystem owns.
By Thursday Jun had turned the functions and the subsystems into an N-squared diagram, printed on a plotter sheet that covered the conference table.

Jun's first N-squared draft. Eight elements run down the diagonal, from structure to Halo Station, and each row shows what that element sends. The air rack's row sends heat to thermal, status to avionics, and cabin air to crew systems. Twenty one of the fifty six cells are marked.

Tiago leaned on the table with both hands and tapped the air rack's row. That one's going to be trouble. Every mess I've ever had in a test cell started in a row like that. Wes wanted to know what anybody planned to do with a chessboard.
Jun's N-squared draft has twenty one of fifty six cells marked. What should the team do with them?
A. Turn each mark into an interface with two owners and a definition.
B. Redraw it as a block diagram with arrows for Wes and the reviewers.
C. Mark only the cells where FRO builds both sides of the link.
D. Put the matrix in the review package and walk the reviewers through it.

Twenty one marks become twenty one entries in an interface register, each with two owners and a blank where the definition goes. Only power and thermal have more marks than the air rack, and those two are FRO's own. Tiago circles the air rack's row in pencil and this time doesn't say anything.

Exactly right. An N-squared diagram finds interfaces systematically: each off-diagonal mark is something one element gives another. Turning marks into managed interfaces, and noticing the most coupled elements, is what makes it worth printing.

The next week Jun moved the architecture into the model. Wes came by while an internal block diagram was on the screen: a block for each subsystem, small squares along their edges, and lines running between the squares.
Ports, Jun said. Where things go in and out. Wes looked at Nadia as if the answer had been a dare. How should the model show HEARTH's physical architecture?
A. Keep the architecture in slides that Wes can edit, one per subsystem.
B. Use block definition diagrams and leave the connections to the ICDs.
C. Model every interface down to its connector pins in the block diagrams now.
D. Add internal block diagrams with typed ports under the block breakdown.

Nadia tells Jun to keep the internal block diagrams under the block breakdown and type every port. He does: 120 volts DC, coolant at a set flow and temperature, a data link, cabin air. When he joins two ports of different types, the line turns red. He does it once on purpose so Wes can see. Huh, Wes says. It argues back.

That's the one. In SysML a block definition diagram shows what the system is made of, and an internal block diagram shows how the parts connect through ports, with typed flows. Typed ports let the model catch a mismatched interface before the hardware does.
Decision five. Where each one lives.
By the end of week seven they were allocating. Each function went to the element that would perform it, and each got a verification point: the place Tiago would prove it worked.

Detect fire went to the fire detection and suppression subsystem. Tiago asked where he should verify it. Nadia picked the cabin smoke sensor in the main air return above the galley. Galleys were where fires started. Helen's had. And all of the cabin's air came back there to the fans. Tiago could hold a calibrated smoke source under it and watch it alarm. It was testable, and it would pass. In the verification point column she typed cabin smoke sensor, verified by test, and they moved to the next row.
The next row was egress. Hatch, Wes said from the doorway. Hatch is structure. Give it to me.
Each function is going to the element that performs it. How should egress be allocated?
A. Allocate egress to every element it needs, with one owner for all of it.
B. Leave egress unallocated until the trade study settles the layout.
C. Spread egress across the elements and let each owner write a share.
D. Allocate egress to structure as Wes asks, with the hatch as its home.

Nadia gives Wes the hatch, but not the whole function. The egress row becomes four rows, each with a derived requirement traced to the parent. Wes gets the hatch and the aisle. Odette gets the alarm, and crew systems gets the lights. Nadia keeps the whole function, and the parent requirement points at all four.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. Allocation assigns functions and requirements to elements. When one function needs several elements, each gets a derived requirement traced to the parent, and somebody still owns the function end to end.

Halo wanted an architecture walkthrough in week eight. Helen wanted to see how a crew moved through the module. The observer from OCSC, the federal office that audits human rating, wanted the hazard controls. Halo's station integrators wanted interfaces. Tiago wanted to know where his test ports would be.
Wes had one answer for all of them. Send them revision C. It's all on there.
Helen, OCSC, the station integrators and Tiago all want different things from the walkthrough. What should FRO show?
A. Send revision C and the N-squared to everyone as one picture.
B. Have each lead build slides for their own audience at the walkthrough.
C. Build each group a view from the model, framed by its concerns.
D. Give every group read access to the whole model and let them search it.

Nadia builds each group its own view from the one model. Five views, each with its viewpoint written down: crew movement, hazard controls, station interfaces, test access, and a structural view for Wes, which he didn't ask for and reads first. They all come from one model, so when the hatch moves, it moves in all five.

Exactly right. Under the architecture description standard, ISO 42010, stakeholders have concerns, a viewpoint sets out how to build a view that frames them, and a view applies it to this system. Views drawn from one model stay consistent.
Halo's interface working group would meet for the first time at the end of week eight, and Amara wanted FRO's interface list presented. You present it, she told Nadia. Jun can run the slides.

Jun had built every line of that list. He'd presented the trace at the SRR, from notes, to people who'd already read it. He'd never had to answer a customer who hadn't. He was already nodding at Amara.

In the hallway afterward he caught up with Nadia. I'd rather run the slides, he said, too fast. Honestly. You know the room. He had the list printed and folded in his back pocket, gone soft at the creases from being opened and closed.
Amara wants FRO's interface list presented at Halo's first working group. Who should present it, and how?
A. Present it herself, and ask Amara to send Jun to a modeling course.
B. Do a dry run with Jun and have him present with her beside him.
C. Present the interface list herself at the working group as Amara asked.
D. Let Jun present it on his own, as the person who built the list.

Nadia asks Jun to present it himself, with her in the chair beside him. They rehearse it twice on Thursday. The second time, Jun stops reading the slides. Afterward they open the competency framework Colleen sent, and Jun picks two to work on, interfaces and communication. He rates himself a supervised practitioner on both. Nadia tells him he's underselling the first one.

That's the one. Human resource management develops people's competencies on the project, not just assigns them. A supported stretch, prepared and backed up, and a plan against a competency framework grow the person and the program.
Decision eight. One box of six.

Halo's station integration lead opened the working group with one slide. HEARTH was a small box on it, one of six: the core module, the power and radiator truss, the robotic arm, a lab module another company was building, the visiting crew vehicles, and the ground. Each box had a different owner and a different contract.
The lead said Halo didn't build any of them. Halo owned the station. Wes leaned over to Nadia. Then who's in charge of ours?

At the break a man on the video wall asked for her by name. He was in a dim room with three screens behind him and a headset pushed down around his neck. Ansel Teague flew the station's robotic arm, for the company that owned it, under contract to Halo. He'd flown arms for nineteen years, most of them on the old station, and he'd be the one holding HEARTH for its last ten meters. He had FRO's interface list up on one of his screens, open to one row: grapple fixture, HEARTH to arm.

Halo moved your berthing this week, he said. Not your fault. A crew vehicle needs that port, so you go later, on a pass where I finish in the dark. Your row says the target on your fixture gets lit by the sun. On the new pass it gets lit by me. My lights bounce off whatever shiny thing you put next to it, and then my camera's looking at glare.
Nadia asked if Halo could move it back.

He smiled a little, the way people do at a question they've heard before. You build the can. I fly the arm. The station decides when. You don't get a vote, and neither do I. He let that sit. So give me something I can see. If I can't see it, I hold your module a meter off the port while three companies argue, and there are people on the other side of that wall.

Nobody had broken anything. The schedule was Halo's. The camera and its lights belonged to Ansel's company. The polished fitting beside the target was FRO's. Each piece was fine on its own. Put together, they were one man at a console trying to find a target in the dark, with HEARTH on the end of his arm.
On Halo's slide, HEARTH sits beside five other boxes with their own owners. How should FRO work within that?
A. Follow Halo's interface spec to the letter and decide the rest at FRO.
B. Ask Halo to take design authority over HEARTH for the station.
C. Get HEARTH right on its own terms for Halo to fit in later.
D. Treat HEARTH as one constituent bound by the station's shared rules.

Nadia writes it at the top of the interface list: FRO owns HEARTH, Halo owns the station's rules and how the station behaves as a whole, and disagreements go to the working group in writing. The integration lead reads it and asks if Halo can borrow the sentence.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. In a system of systems, each constituent keeps its own owner and management. The SoS authority sets the shared rules and owns the behavior that only exists across constituents. Know where your authority ends.

At the start of week nine Halo issued a station change. Every module would use the station's caution and warning tones and the station's panel, so a crew member heard one alarm language wherever they were. HEARTH's own alarm, which Helen had chosen to be heard in every quarter, was out.
Odette brought the page to Nadia's desk. One alarm language in every module. That's the right rule, she said. We picked ours so you'd hear it through a curtain, though. I want theirs to do the same.
Halo's station change replaces HEARTH's own alarm with the station's tones. How should FRO respond?
A. Adopt the station tones as issued and log the audibility question.
B. Keep HEARTH's own alarm, which Helen chose for every quarter.
C. Adopt the station alarm and check it's heard in every bunk.
D. Hold the change until Halo issues a paid contract modification.

Nadia takes the station's alarm and asks for one proof: it has to be heard in every bunk. Jun traces the change: the alarm function, two interfaces and the audibility requirement. The station tones run a little quieter than HEARTH's. Nadia writes it up, and Halo agrees to a louder speaker in HEARTH inside the station's rules. Helen signs off on the speaker herself.

Exactly right. Station-wide behavior belongs to the SoS authority, so HEARTH follows the shared rule. As a constituent, its job is to assess the impact on its own requirements and settle conflicts formally, not ignore the rule or quietly lose a need.

Tiago caught Nadia in the high bay with a draft test procedure in one hand. Every number in here I typed from the requirements PDF. If one changes, I won't know. Wes's CAD won't know either. The model knows, and that's it.

Jun had ideas about that, and he had them at length. His roommate wrote discharge forecasting software at Halcyon AI, across town, and Jun liked to point out that his own model only had to predict a hatch.
Tiago types every number in his procedures from the requirements PDF. What should tie the data together?
A. Export a weekly snapshot of the model for everyone's copies.
B. Wait for CDR, when the design is stable, to link up all the tools.
C. Link requirements, model, CAD and test steps by ID, interfaces first.
D. Move requirements, the model, CAD and test procedures into one new tool.

Jun and Tiago wire up the first links in a week. Each test step points to the requirement it checks, and each requirement to the model element and the drawing where it lives. Wes changes a hatch dimension on Thursday. By Friday two of Tiago's test steps are flagged. Okay, he says. That's worth something.

That's the one. A digital thread connects authoritative data across the life cycle, so a change can be followed to everything it touches. Starting with the riskiest links gets value early without trying to connect everything at once.

Tamarack's proposal gave one number for the heat the air rack would dump into HEARTH's coolant loop. Jun wanted to know whether the loop could take it in every mode the crew would use. Amara wanted the answer by Friday.
Use their number, she said. It's in a signed proposal. Tiago, passing with a cart, said thermal vacuum testing would settle it for sure in about two years.
Jun asks whether HEARTH's coolant loop can take the air rack's heat. How should the team find out?
A. Order a full computer model of the cabin's heat and airflow first.
B. Run a heat balance mode by mode, writing down each assumption.
C. Wait for thermal vacuum testing to measure the real rack.
D. Check Tamarack's proposal number against the loop's full capacity.

Jun builds a heat balance for each mode in two days: sleep, nominal, exercise, and a hot orbit. The loop holds in all of them except exercise in a hot orbit, where it's tight. At the top of the page he writes: rack heat from Tamarack proposal, not design data. Nadia circles that line.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. System analysis gives decision makers data they can trust: the right question, detail matched to the decision, assumptions and uncertainty stated. Its results feed architecture and design.

Halo sent its interface requirements for the berthing mechanism, station power, data and the radiator loop. The same afternoon Pavel Ruzicka at Tamarack sent an email. Their rack came from the same family they'd flown on the old station, he wrote. It would drop right in, and the details could be sorted out at integration, the way they always had been.

The grapple fixture's section of Halo's package carried a line Ansel had asked for, in plain words: nothing shiny within a meter of the target. The fitting beside the target was Wes's. Stainless, a bracket for the fixture's cover, and Wes had called it out polished, number eight finish, same as every cover bracket on the cargo modules. There was one on his desk holding down a stack of drawings. Nadia set the printout next to it and the overhead lights came right back off it into her eyes, which was more or less the point she'd come down to make.
Wes read the line, then read it again. I polish those so I can see a crack, he said. Bench lamp, tilt it, crack shows. You blast it gray, you're looking at sandpaper.

Ansel's looking at it on his own lights, at night, with people on the other side of the wall, Nadia said. The lights were bolted to the arm next to the camera, she told him, so they pointed wherever it did. She had Ansel's row up on her phone. If he couldn't find the target he'd hold HEARTH a meter off the port while three companies argued about it.
Wes didn't take the phone. So I fly a part I can't inspect so a man I've never met doesn't get glare.
So we berth, she said. You inspect it some other way.

He thought about it long enough that she figured she'd lost. Then he said Penetrant, like he'd been made to eat something. Dye penetrant on every bracket before finishing, then a bead blast after, which was about a day per part, and nobody had a line for it in the schedule. He wrote PENETRANT FIRST, NO BRIGHT FINISH WITHIN ONE METER OF TARGET on the back of her printout in his square capitals and slid it back across the desk. My name goes on that one. The day goes on Amara's. Then he put the bracket in his drawer.
Back at her desk, Jun's list had twenty one interfaces. Eleven had a definition both sides had signed.
Pavel says Tamarack's rack will drop right in, with details sorted at integration. How should its interfaces be handled?
A. Use ICDs for the station and a Tamarack datasheet for the rack.
B. Let Tamarack define the rack's interfaces and fit HEARTH to them.
C. Run Halo's interfaces through ICDs and settle Tamarack's on email with Pavel.
D. Bring the rack's interfaces under signed ICDs, the same as the station's.

Nadia puts the rack's interfaces under signed interface control documents, ICDs, the same as the station's. Halo's integration lead takes the station side. Pavel agrees, sounding a little hurt, to send Tamarack's interface data by the end of the week. Every row on the list has two owners and a due date.

Exactly right. Interface management identifies, defines, controls and verifies interfaces, with both sides agreeing to an ICD that goes under configuration control. Supplier interfaces need it as much as outside ones.
At the end of week eight Jun had presented FRO's interface list to Halo's working group himself. When Halo's lead asked who owned the rack coolant interface, he answered without looking at Nadia.
On Friday Tamarack's interface data arrived.
It came in on the date Jun had asked for, with Pavel's name at the bottom. Jun loaded it into the model that afternoon.
He gave the rack a block in the model, typed its ports from Pavel's data, and connected them to HEARTH's. Three of the four lines turned red.

Jun's interface check on Tamarack's air rack. Power doesn't match: the rack takes 28 volts DC, and HEARTH distributes 120 volts DC. Coolant doesn't match: the rack's quick disconnects are one size smaller than HEARTH's, on the opposite face of the rack. Data doesn't match: the rack's on a fifteen fifty three bus, and HEARTH's avionics are on Ethernet. Only the mounting points match.
Jun looked at the screen and then at her. It doesn't plug in, he said. Not one of the three.

Wes read the three red lines standing up and didn't say drop right in, though she could see him think it. When you call Pavel, he said, I want to be on the line. I've plugged his racks into things before.
Nadia went to the whiteboard. The 133 was still there in its red box. Under it she wrote RACK: POWER, COOLANT, DATA.
She opened a new email to Pavel and wrote the first line before she could think of a kinder one.
